title: Pauri 37, meaning: grace and truth
hook: in the realm of grace dwell the mighty in spirit; in the realm of truth dwells the Formless, beholding all (Japji 37)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 37, hor. Your line was karam khandd, the realm of grace. Did one unearned good thing come your way? Today, the grace realm opened, and the last realm of all. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

Try this. Describe your mother's voice, or your grandfather's laugh, to someone who never heard it. A few words come: warm, a bit low, it cracks at the end. And then the words run out, because they're so much smaller than the thing. The trouble isn't knowing it. It's that knowing and telling are different skills, and some things only allow one of them. Two stanzas ago, Saram Khand already warned that its matters can't be told. Pauri 37 climbs to the very top of the Japji's ladder, and at the end of it, Guru Nanak meets that wall again, harder than before.
screen: `DESCRIBE A VOICE YOU LOVE.` → `THE WORDS ARE TOO SMALL.` → `KNOWING ISN'T TELLING.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: in the realm of grace, the language is power, and there is no one else. Who lives there? Tithai jodh mahaabal soor. Warriors of great strength, heroes, and the Lord, here called Raam, a name the Granth uses for the One who fills everything, is completely present in them. They neither die nor are deceived, the stanza says, those in whose minds the One lives. Devotees of many worlds dwell there, full of joy, the True One in their hearts. That's the fourth realm, Karam Khand. Then the fifth, the top of the ladder: sach khandd vasai nirankaar. In the realm of truth dwells the Formless One. Sach Khand. And what does the Formless do there? Kar kar vekhai nadar nihaal. Creating, He watches over it all, and blesses with a glance. You've heard that watching before, in Pauris 30 and 31. Here it's at home. In Sach Khand, the stanza says, there are continents and worlds and universes without end; worlds upon worlds of forms, each moving as the order moves it. He sees, He is delighted, He reflects. And then Nanak stops. Nanak kathnaa karrarraa saar. To describe it is as hard as steel. Saar is steel, iron. You could chew on it forever and not bite through. That's today's line. In Pauri 36 the words fell short; here they meet steel. Some Sikh teachers describe Sach Khand not only as a place after this life but as a state to be touched now, in the heart, when the Formless is near.
screen: `KARAM KHAND — THE MIGHTY IN SPIRIT.` · `SACH KHAND — THE FORMLESS DWELLS.` · `HE WATCHES, BLESSING WITH A GLANCE.` · `KATHNAA KARRARRAA SAAR.` · then, large: `HARD AS STEEL TO TELL.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and bring to mind the things you're grateful for, one at a time, without describing them. A face. A meal. A morning. A voice. Don't find the words. Just let each one arrive, and feel the thanks, and let it go. If a word does come, fine; let it pass. Keep going quietly, one gift after another, until the bell. When the list runs out, just rest in the thanks itself. The bell holds the time.
Sach Khand. The realm of truth, where the Formless One dwells, creating and watching with a kindly glance. The fifth realm, the top of the ladder, and too hard to tell.
Your line: hard as steel to tell. Today, when you can't find words for something that moves you, let the silence be enough. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 37 describes Karam Khand, the realm of grace, and Sach Khand, the realm of truth where the Formless dwells, and ends with Nanak saying that describing it is as hard as steel.

fork.setup: you've reached the top of the ladder, Sach Khand. you're asked to describe it. what does Nanak do?

says only the yogis can describe it.
fork.reveal: Nanak kathnaa karrarraa saar. the top of the ladder ends with steel, not a map.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 37: in the realm of truth dwells the Formless.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sach Khand is heaven.
what it means: the realm of truth where the Formless dwells, which some Sikh teachers describe as a state to touch now as well as after death.
what a scholar hears: saar is steel or iron; the stanza reuses kar kar vekhai from Pauri 31 and closes the five khands on an admission that words fail.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8 (Japji, Pauri 37, last line)

notes: Gurmukhi quoted in transliteration as the original; English is paraphrase. Macauliffe 1909 not quoted because not verified word for word.
Raam explained as a name the Granth uses for the all-pervading One; confirm wording.
The line 'seeto seetaa mahimaa maahi' is omitted because its readings differ widely; the Keeper may want it addressed.
Sach Khand as both a state now and a realm after death is presented as what 'some Sikh teachers' describe; confirm.

Editor review: the hook and teach no longer repeat day 225's 'words fall short' angle as new; they now name the echo of Pauri 36 and build on it; dropped 'an honest admission' (used on day 225) and the hook's line telling the listener how well they know a voice; replaced a myth that repeated day 225's and the 'many Sikhs' myth with two items from the stanza's grace lines.
